newsitem.title: USA: Mass. AG slams tobacco firms for alleged shredding.
newsitem.headline: Mass. AG slams tobacco firms for alleged shredding.

text.p: Massachusetts Attorney General Scott Harshbarger said Sunday that testimony from a former Philip Morris Co. Inc. chemist bolsters the need for the state's first-in-the-nation tobacco disclosure law.

"These must be the so-called 'trade secrets' the industry is working so hard to conceal by trying to derail our ingredient disclosure law," Harshbarger said in a statement. "This testimony is some of the strongest evidence yet of Big Tobacco's efforts to hide the truth about their products."

Testimony regarding the alleged shredding came from William Raymond Morgan, who worked as an analytical chemist for Philip Morris, during a deposition last week as part of pre-trial preparations by the state of Texas. That state, like Massachusetts and 19 other states and cities, is suing the industry in an effort to recover money spent by taxpayers to treat indigent citizens suffering from tobacco related illnesses.

In a deposition, 20-year Philip Morris analytical chemist Ray Morgan said he was ordered in the 1980s to shred research reports that showed "alarmingly high" concentrations of nitrosamine, a known carcinogen, in tobacco smoke, Texas Attorney General Dan Morales said on Thursday.

Morgan also testified that the company, a unit of Philip Morris Cos. Inc., used "non-production" cigarettes with fewer chemical additives than cigarettes sold to consumers in research tests used to detect carcinogens, Morales said.

A Massachusetts law expected to go into effect on July 1 will require all tobacco companies to list the ingredients by weight or measure of each brand of their cigarettes and smokeless tobacco products sold in the state with the Department of Public Health. The department is to then make those lists available to the public.

Four tobacco companies, including Philip Morris, are challenging the law in federal court. But the four, which include R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp., Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc, and Lorillard Tobacco Co., a unit of Loews Corp., lost the first part of their fight late last month when a federal judge ruled public hearings on the issue could go forward.

"The type of chemical additive allegedly discovered in these tests is exactly the kind of ingredient that would be made public by our disclosure law," said Harshbarger, who is representing the state in the federal action.
Phone calls to Philip Morris seeking comment were not immediately returned.
